title: Introduction to Shiny
text:
Shiny lets you turn R code into an interactive web application: the user clicks, chooses and uploads, and R does the computations behind the scenes.
In this course we start from an empty RStudio project and finish with your own app online, with a link you can send to anyone.

title: Interactive plots
text: A plot can also be used as an input. Try it: choose a dataset, click Load data, then Select & Display, and finally click on a point or draw a rectangle on the plot.

title: Interactive plots
text:
How it works
A plotOutput() can also be an input: if you give it the click and brush arguments, the coordinates of a click, or of the rectangle drawn with the mouse, arrive in the server as input$plot_click and input$plot_brush.
plotOutput("graph",
1           click = clickOpts(id = "plot_click"),
2           brush = brushOpts(id = "plot_brush"))

1

A click on the plot → input$plot_click

2

A rectangle drawn on the plot → input$plot_brush


Two helpers turn the coordinates into rows of the data:
nearPoints(df, input$plot_click, xvar = "speed", yvar = "dist")      # rows close to the click
brushedPoints(df, input$plot_brush, xvar = "speed", yvar = "dist")   # rows inside the rectangle

title: Interactive plots
text:
The code
#| '!! shinylive warning !!': |
#|   shinylive does not work in self-contained HTML documents.
#|   Please set `embed-resources: false` in your metadata.
#| standalone: true
#| components: [editor, viewer]
#| layout: vertical
#| viewerHeight: 750
## file: ui.R
library(shiny)

ui <- fluidPage(
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      selectInput("dataset", "Choose a dataset:",
                  choices = c("rock", "pressure", "cars")),
      actionButton("load", "Load data"),
      conditionalPanel(
        condition = "input.load >= 1",       # shown after the first click
        uiOutput("var1"),
        uiOutput("var2"),
        actionButton("select", "Select & Display")
      )
    ),
    mainPanel(
      plotOutput(
        "graph",
        click = clickOpts(id = "plot_click"),  # click -> input$plot_click
        brush = brushOpts(id = "plot_brush")   # drag  -> input$plot_brush
      ),
      fluidRow(
        column(4, verbatimTextOutput("summary")),
        column(4, verbatimTextOutput("points")),
        column(4, verbatimTextOutput("brush"))
      )
    )
  )
)

## file: server.R
library(shiny)

server <- function(input, output, session) {

  # reactiveValues: a "shelf" where we put objects and change them later
  values <- reactiveValues()

  observeEvent(input$load, {
    values$data <- switch(input$dataset,
                          rock = rock,
                          pressure = pressure,
                          cars = cars)
  })

  output$var1 <- renderUI({
    nam <- names(values$data)
    selectInput("var1", "Select x:", choices = nam, selected = nam[1])
  })

  output$var2 <- renderUI({
    nam <- names(values$data)
    selectInput("var2", "Select y:", choices = nam, selected = nam[2])
  })

  observeEvent(input$select, {
    values$df <- values$data[, c(input$var1, input$var2)]
  })

  output$graph <- renderPlot({
    validate(need(input$select > 0, "Waiting for data"))
    plot(values$df[, 1:2])
  })

  output$summary <- renderPrint({
    validate(need(input$select > 0, "Waiting for data"))
    summary(values$df)
  })

  output$points <- renderPrint({
    req(values$df)
    pointID <- nearPoints(values$df, input$plot_click,
                          xvar = names(values$df)[1],
                          yvar = names(values$df)[2])
    validate(need(nrow(pointID) != 0, "Click on a point"))
    pointID
  })

  output$brush <- renderPrint({
    req(values$df)
    brushID <- brushedPoints(values$df, input$plot_brush,
                             xvar = names(values$df)[1],
                             yvar = names(values$df)[2])
    validate(need(nrow(brushID) != 0, "Highlight an area"))
    brushID
  })
}

title: Wait for it: eventReactive()
text:
With reactive(), the app reacts immediately to every change. That is not always what we want:
We want the app to wait until the user says “go”. The “go” is an actionButton(), and the waiting is done by eventReactive().

title: Wait for it: eventReactive()
text:
The app
Change the dataset: nothing happens. Click the button: now it does.
#| '!! shinylive warning !!': |
#|   shinylive does not work in self-contained HTML documents.
#|   Please set `embed-resources: false` in your metadata.
#| standalone: true
#| components: [viewer]
#| viewerHeight: 650
## file: ui.R
library(shiny)

ui <- fluidPage(
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      selectInput(
        inputId = "dataset",
        label = "Choose a dataset:",
        choices = c("rock", "pressure", "cars")
      ),
      actionButton("load", "Select dataset")
    ),
    mainPanel(
      plotOutput("graph"),
      verbatimTextOutput("summary")
    )
  )
)

## file: server.R
library(shiny)

server <- function(input, output, session) {

  # runs ONLY when the button is clicked
  dataInput <- eventReactive(input$load, {
    switch(input$dataset,
           rock = rock,
           pressure = pressure,
           cars = cars)
  })

  output$graph <- renderPlot({
    data <- dataInput()
    plot(data[, 1:2])
  })

  output$summary <- renderPrint({
    data <- dataInput()
    summary(data[, 1:2])
  })
}

Notice also that before the first click the outputs are empty: at the start the button has never been clicked, so eventReactive() has no value yet, and the outputs that need it wait silently.

text:
The two pieces
# ui.R

2    switch(input$dataset,

1

The first argument is the trigger: the code runs only when input$load changes, i.e., when the button is clicked

2

The code to run. It reads input$dataset, but changing the dataset does not trigger it: its value is simply read at the moment of the click

title: Outputs and render functions
text:
renderText() or renderPrint()?
They look similar but they are not the same:

renderText() turns the result into one plain string (it uses cat()): good for sentences
renderPrint() shows the result as the R console would print it: good for summary(), str(), models, data frames

In the app above, replace renderPrint with renderText for summary(data) (and verbatimTextOutput with textOutput in the UI): the numbers are all glued together. That is why we use renderPrint() for statistical output.

title: Outputs and render functions
text:
Common mistakes






When the box stays empty




The IDs do not match: plotOutput("graph") in the UI, output$grahp in the server. No error, just an empty box
The pair is wrong: plotOutput() in the UI, renderPrint() in the server. The box cannot show that content
You forgot output$...: renderPlot({ ... }) alone computes the plot and throws it away
The box is not in the UI: the server fills output$summary, but ui.R has no ...Output("summary")

text: The Shiny page showed the logic: the UI sets the options and displays the results, the server elaborates the options and sends back the results. Here we look inside the two pieces, and at how they talk to each other.

section: The UI is a web page

title: How Shiny thinks
text:
The server is a function
server <- function(input, output, session) {
  ...
}
Shiny calls this function once for each user that opens the app (each user has their own session). Inside it:

input is a list with the current value of every input, accessed by ID: input$mySelection. You can read it, you cannot change it
output is the list of the boxes to fill, accessed by ID: output$myOutput <- render…({ … })

title: How Shiny thinks
text:
The contract: IDs
Let’s go back to the first app. Use it once more, then we follow the IDs in the code:

    label = h3("Select box"),           # what the user reads
    choices = list("Choice 1" = 1, "Choice 2" = 2, "Choice 3" = 3),
    selected = 1

The rules of the contract

Defined in the UI, not used in the server: nothing happens. The widget is there, you can play with it, but nobody is listening
Used in the server, not defined in the UI (often a typo!): Shiny does not warn you

input$myselection (lowercase s) simply is NULL, so the result is empty or the code fails
output$myOuptut is computed but never shown, because no box has that name

IDs must be unique: two elements with the same ID make the app behave unpredictably (outputs may not show at all)
input is read-only: input$mySelection <- 2 is an error

title: How Shiny thinks
text:
Reactivity: the mental model
The server contains no loop, no “when the user clicks, do this”. How does the output change when the input changes?
Think of a spreadsheet. If cell B1 contains =A1 * 2, you never “run” B1: every time A1 changes, B1 updates by itself.
render*() functions work the same way:

the code inside render*({ ... }) is a recipe, not a command executed once
Shiny notes which inputs the recipe reads (here: input$mySelection)
when one of those inputs changes, Shiny re-runs the recipe and sends the new result to the box






flowchart LR
    I["input$mySelection<br/>changes"] --> R["renderPrint({ ... })<br/>runs again"] --> O["output$myOutput<br/>is updated"]
    style I fill:#2b6c8e,color:#fff
    style R fill:#8fd36f,color:#fff
    style O fill:#2b6c8e,color:#fff






This is why the server is not read from top to bottom like a script: each recipe runs when it needs to.






Inputs live only inside reactive code



Reading an input outside a recipe does not work:
server <- function(input, output, session) {
  choice <- input$mySelection        # ❌ outside render*()
  output$myOutput <- renderPrint({ choice })
}
Error: Can't access reactive value 'mySelection' outside of reactive consumer.
The server function runs once, at the start: at that moment nobody has chosen anything yet. Inputs must be read inside render*() (or the other reactive functions we will meet: reactive(), eventReactive()).








In a nutshell




UI = what the user sees: inputs (controls) and outputs (empty boxes)
Server = a function of input and output that fills the boxes
They talk only through IDs: inputId → input$id, outputId → output$id
render*() are recipes that re-run automatically when the inputs they read change

text:
A Shiny app is a folder. In the folder there are (at least) two R scripts:
The best way to keep that folder tidy is an RStudio project. RStudio has a specific type of project for Shiny apps, which comes with a ready-made (and pretty basic) app.
This project will also become the GitHub repository that, on Day 2, is uploaded to the server to make the app shareable and online.

title: A Shiny project
text:
Step 1 · Create a Shiny project
In RStudio:

File → New Project… → New Directory → Shiny Application
Directory name: my-shiny-app (no spaces, no accents)
Choose where to save it (e.g., Documents/GitHub) and click Create Project

Step 2 · Create ui.R and server.R
The default Shiny Project creates an extremely basic app using the Old Faithful Geyser data. The code is stored in a single file named called app.R:

Step 4 · Run the app
As soon as a file called ui.R or server.R is open, RStudio replaces the usual Run button with ▶ Run App. Click it.
What happens:

In the console you read something like Listening on http://127.0.0.1:4321: R has started a small web server on your computer
A window (or a browser tab) opens with the app: that is the UI, turned into a web page
The console shows a red stop sign: R is busy serving the app, so you cannot use the console until you stop it

shinyapps.io is the “official” server for shiny apps. The free licence version allows for hosting 5 apps at the time.






Connect cloud



At the end of 2026, shinyapps.io will be replaced by Connect Cloud







Connect cloud landing page and account creation


The account on Connect Cloud can be connected to an already existent account, such as a Google Account. The best option is to link Connect Cloud to your GitHub account:



Link Connect Cloud to your GitHub account


Follow the instructions and then choose an account name for posit.




The app must be stored in an R file with clearly defined ui and server.
The R file must be named app.R.
Once the app is ready for deployment, commit and push as usual.






Before the deploy: one file called app.R



Connect Cloud wants the ui and the server in the same file, and the file must be called app.R. Our project has two files, ui.R and server.R: there are two ways to get to app.R.
Option 1 · Keep ui.R and server.R, and add a small app.R
File → New File → R Script, paste this and save it as app.R in the project folder, next to ui.R and server.R:
library(shiny)

source("ui.R")        # creates the object ui
source("server.R")    # creates the object server

shinyApp(ui, server)
source() runs the two files, so the objects ui and server are ready for shinyApp(). When you change the app, you keep working on ui.R and server.R as before.
Option 2 · Put everything in app.R
Create a new script app.R and copy into it the content of ui.R and server.R, one after the other, then add shinyApp() at the end:
library(shiny)

# content of ui.R
ui = fluidPage(
  ...
)

# content of server.R
server = function(input, output) {
  ...
}

shinyApp(ui, server)
library(shiny) is needed only once, at the top. Then delete ui.R and server.R, so that there is only one version of the app.
Either way, check that app.R works with Run App before going on.


The file must be within an R project, which is set to be a GitHub repository.



The rsconnect package is necessary to link the local app, the GitHub repository, and the Connect Cloud.
Connect Cloud is not R – as such, it needs external files describing the packages/dependencies that are employed and needed for the app deployment.
First, the package needs to be installed (Listing 1).



Listing 1: Install the package, run only once.


install.packages("rsconnect")



Then, within the R-project hosting the app.R file, run the code in Listing 2.



Listing 2: Write the manifest


rsconnect::writeManifest()



The file manifest.json appears within the R project, making the app deployment possible.






manifest.json



manifest.json is the “shopping list” of your app. It records which version of R the app uses, which packages it needs (with their exact versions) and which files belong to the app. Connect Cloud is not your computer and has none of your packages installed: it reads the manifest and installs exactly those packages before starting the app. If you add a package to the app, you have to run rsconnect::writeManifest() again.


For the deployment, the folder of the project should have the following structure:
app-Examples/
├── .gitattributes
├── .gitignore
├── app-Examples.Rproj
├── app.R
└── manifest.json



Everything is ready for the actual deployment of the app from Connect Cloud.
From the Home of your profile, search for the Publish button:








Figure 1: Publish button on Connect Cloud.





Select the repository, the folder, and the specific file of the app (Figure 2)






Figure 2: Deploy app and publish it

text: fluidPage() is a page based on a grid 12 units wide. On top of it, Shiny offers a few ready-made structures.

title: Layouts
text:
See them
A sidebar, three tabs, and two columns inside the last tab. Click on the tabs:

## file: ui.R
library(shiny)

ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("Layouts"),
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      selectInput("dataset", "Choose a dataset:",
                  choices = c("rock", "pressure", "cars")),
      width = 3                       # the sidebar takes 3 of 12 units
    ),
    mainPanel(
      tabsetPanel(
        tabPanel("Plot", plotOutput("plot")),
        tabPanel("Summary", verbatimTextOutput("summary")),
        tabPanel("Two columns",
                 fluidRow(

                   column(6, h4("Second column"), plotOutput("hist", height = "250px"))

)
## file: server.R
library(shiny)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  dataInput <- reactive(get(input$dataset))

  output$plot    <- renderPlot(plot(dataInput()[, 1:2]))
  output$summary <- renderPrint(summary(dataInput()))
  output$head    <- renderTable(head(dataInput()))
  output$hist    <- renderPlot(hist(dataInput()[, 1], main = names(dataInput())[1]))

text:
In Your app: explore a dataset the X and Y menus were created by the server with renderUI(). There is another way: the menus exist in ui.R from the start, empty, and the server updates their choices when the data are loaded.

text:
How it works
# ui.R
1selectInput("x", "X variable:", choices = NULL)

1

A normal menu, with no choices yet


# server.R
1server <- function(input, output, session) {

2  observeEvent(dataInput(), {

3    updateSelectInput(session, "x", choices = vars)

title: Updating inputs
text:
The code
#| '!! shinylive warning !!': |
#|   shinylive does not work in self-contained HTML documents.
#|   Please set `embed-resources: false` in your metadata.
#| standalone: true
#| components: [editor, viewer]
#| layout: vertical
#| viewerHeight: 700
## file: ui.R
library(shiny)

ui <- fluidPage(
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      selectInput("dataset", "Choose a dataset:",
                  choices = c("rock", "pressure", "cars")),
      actionButton("load", "Load dataset"),
      hr(),
      # the menus exist from the start, but they are empty
      selectInput("x", "X variable:", choices = NULL),
      selectInput("y", "Y variable:", choices = NULL),
      actionButton("analyze", "Update analysis")
    ),
    mainPanel(
      plotOutput("graph"),
      verbatimTextOutput("summary")
    )
  )
)

## file: server.R
library(shiny)

server <- function(input, output, session) {   # session is needed by update*()

  dataInput <- eventReactive(input$load, {
    switch(input$dataset,
           rock = rock,
           pressure = pressure,
           cars = cars)
  })

  # observeEvent: DO something (a side effect) when the data change.
  # It returns nothing: it updates the menus that already exist in the UI
  observeEvent(dataInput(), {
    vars <- names(dataInput())
    updateSelectInput(session, "x", choices = vars, selected = vars[1])
    updateSelectInput(session, "y", choices = vars,
                      selected = vars[min(2, length(vars))])
  })

  # freeze data + chosen variables when "Update analysis" is clicked
  analysisInput <- eventReactive(input$analyze, {
    req(input$x, input$y)
    list(data = dataInput(), x = input$x, y = input$y)
  })

  output$graph <- renderPlot({
    obj <- analysisInput()
    plot(obj$data[[obj$x]], obj$data[[obj$y]],
         xlab = obj$x, ylab = obj$y, pch = 19)
  })

  output$summary <- renderPrint({
    obj <- analysisInput()
    summary(obj$data[, c(obj$x, obj$y)])
  })
}

title: Updating inputs
section: req(): wait for what you need
text:
req(): wait for what you need
In this app analysisInput() starts with req(input$x, input$y). req() checks that its arguments are “available” (not NULL, not empty, not FALSE…). If they are not, it stops the computation silently: no red error, the output simply waits.
Use it whenever an output needs something that may not be there yet: an uploaded file, a selection, a click.
